```js
import jQuery from 'jquery';
import KimaiReducedClickHandler from "./KimaiReducedClickHandler";
```

The class is exported on line 18:

```js
export default class KimaiAjaxModalForm extends KimaiReducedClickHandler {
```

So start with `KimaiAjaxModalForm` itself, then go back to `KimaiReducedClickHandler` to understand its existing click-handling context. The parent class implementation is not excerpted on this page; the relationships this file explicitly establishes are just the inheritance and these two imports. At least one call to `jquery` can be located directly in this file, in the lookup for the form's autofocus element.

The most compact view of the local relationships identified so far is:

```text
KimaiReducedClickHandler
          |

KimaiAjaxModalForm
  |                    |
  v                    v
getContainer()      _getFormIdentifier()
  |                    |
  v                    v
getTranslation()    jQuery(...).find('[autofocus]')
  |
  v
get('modal.dirty')
```

This diagram expands only the expressions already located in the file. The call chain on the left and the jQuery lookup on the right appear together, but they are not the same variable, and there is no reason to merge them into a single "message matching" path in these notes.

On line 30, `const self = this;` is an alias used by subsequent local references. Immediately after it is:

```js
const msg = self.getContainer().getTranslation().get('modal.dirty');
```

Record the source of `msg` as the container-provided translation object, together with the key passed to `get()`: `modal.dirty`. The first draft put this line and the later flash identifiers in the same paragraph, making it sound as though the final location where the message appears had already been confirmed; that grouping went too far. After review, keep the conclusion narrower: the text key is read here, while `flashErrorIdentifier` and `flashMessageIdentifier` are names declared separately later in the file.

The focus-related code is more precisely located. Line 58 reads:

```js
let formAutofocus = jQuery(self._getFormIdentifier()).find('[autofocus]');
```

It is still worth keeping the locations of the three identifiers as a separate note: `formIdentifier` is near line 103, and `flashErrorIdentifier` and `flashMessageIdentifier` are near lines 105 and 107, respectively. # History of empty duration handling and monthly statistics

## Starting point

This record starts by putting two neighboring issues side by side: whether the existing begin and end can define an interval when a time entry has no explicit duration; and how query endpoints are positioned at the start and end of a month for monthly statistics. Both involve time, but they are not the same decision.

Two approaches were initially compared. The first was to continue requiring every caller to submit duration. This would spare the object itself from having to interpret an empty value, but different entry points might produce time entries with different shapes. The second was to derive elapsed time from the existing start and end times when the explicit value was empty. The latter was closer to the interval already shown on the page, but only if both endpoints were present.

At the time, the second approach was tentatively preferred, but it was not set down as a universal rule. Records with only begin or only end were still a different class of input; an empty duration did not mean they could be grouped with computable intervals.

This choice was not yet to be applied to monthly statistics. Examples within a single month made differences in the end point hard to see; only records spanning months would reveal whether both the end of the month and the start of the next month were included. The meaning of a closed interval was left for further review.

The earlier investigation started at `public/build/calendar.52d75f80.js`. The notes contain terms such as duration, null, begin, end, and interval, making them useful for revisiting the snippets around the page at the time; they did not preserve the relationships involved in the monthly statistics implementation. Next time, an input time, the resulting interval, and the month it belongs to need to be saved together, not just the total on the page.

# Null duration and the evolution of monthly statistics

## Two questions left from the start

The early notes kept two questions side by side: how to obtain a duration for a time entry with no explicit duration, and how to define the end boundary for monthly statistics. There was a practical reason for this: both investigations involved begin, end, and interval. Later review found that keeping them together did not mean the same reasoning could answer both.

There were two candidates for the null-value branch. One was to keep the requirement that callers supply duration and leave null values as null. This option would require only limited changes, but the available material did not establish whether all read paths could provide the same fields. The other was to use the elapsed time between begin and end as the duration when both were present. The first draft treated this only as a direction to verify and did not specify a default when an endpoint was missing.

The monthly part also had two candidates: use the start of the next month as the end of this month's filter, or use the last instant that could be included in this month. Full-month records might show no difference between the two formulations; a cross-month record is what makes the endpoint choice visible. This review therefore did not take "closed interval" as a settled implementation detail.

## Reviewing the input shapes

The review split time entries into three groups by input:

- An explicit duration is present;
- duration is null, but both begin and end are present;
- Only one time point is present, or the available time objects are insufficient to form an interval.

The first group should not be reinterpreted by the null-value logic. The second deserves a separate check because it is not missing time information, only the saved explicit duration. For the third group, elapsed seconds cannot be derived from the known fields. Setting the third group directly to zero would collapse "a duration that is genuinely zero" and "incomplete input" into one result, leaving no way to distinguish them when reviewing anomalous records later.

This breakdown corrected one statement in the early notes. Those notes simplified "null duration" to "no duration"; we retain the original term but no longer use that interpretation. It is the explicit field that is null, which does not necessarily mean there is no elapsed time between begin and end.

The review did not address cases where an explicit duration conflicts with the start and end times. Those are conflicting values, not counterexamples to the null-value branch. Deciding precedence here would insert an unconfirmed model rule into a local check.

## The old investigation sequence, retained

The old notes said: read duration first; if it is null, read begin; then fill in end from the calendar results; finally pass the number of seconds to monthly statistics.

This sequence remains here, but is no longer the default procedure. The issue is not that calendar data is necessarily useless, but that the sequence assumes every entry point goes through the same page data source. The old investigation reference `public/build/calendar.52d75f80.js` can help locate the snippets about duration, null, begin, and end from that time, but it is not enough to establish that end is necessarily filled in there, or that monthly statistics are part of that build artifact.

The old steps also blurred a second distinction: passing the seconds straight to monthly statistics made it look as though the interval calculation had already determined the month for the report. In fact, elapsed seconds and month assignment each require inputs. The former depends on at least two time points; the latter also depends on how query endpoints are interpreted for cross-month records.

## Limitations of a trial calculation

The trial changed only one condition: it kept begin and end but did not supply an explicit duration. The record contains no complete execution output, only search traces for `getDuration()` and a note to do a manual calculation from 10:00 to 11:30. This is enough to indicate that the review should focus on where duration is accessed, rather than first working backward from the monthly total; it is not enough to specify a recovery method for every missing field.

The trial ruled out one premature diagnosis. If the statistics layer is already receiving a null or incorrect value, an abnormal monthly display cannot first be attributed to month filtering. The interval calculation should be checked independently first, before discussing which monthly query includes the record.

The trial did not answer the cross-month case either. A record running from month-end into the next month may involve elapsed seconds or month assignment, but neither determines the other. Without cross-month input and returned results, no closed-interval formulation can be called the common convention for all reports.

## Review addendum

The review revisited where to place the derivation. Placing it near the calendar data source gives page drag-and-drop access to complete data earlier, but other read paths may bypass it. Placing it near Timesheet's duration access avoids each caller having to duplicate the null check, but requires strict handling of input shapes where begin or end is missing.

The decision is to record these two choices separately: retain the calendar build artifact as an old investigation entry point; focus first on Timesheet's duration access when reviewing what null duration means. This does not settle whether the calendar entry point is still used by all pages.

The meeting's margin notes also preserve an order of checks: first confirm a record's inputs and interval result, then put that same record through the month check. This is not the complete rule for report queries, nor does it mean calculation can continue when end is missing.

## Provisional boundaries for the monthly part

For monthly statistics, only the scope of the checks has been set, not the final closed-interval formulation. Whether the first instant of the next month belongs to the previous month cannot be inferred directly from a verbal description such as "the last second of this month"; likewise, a full-month example cannot distinguish between endpoint formulations.

The next review should keep these side by side: a record with begin and end present but duration null; a cross-month record; a record exactly at the start of the next month; and a record missing an endpoint. Both elapsed seconds for the interval and the reporting month must be visible for each. Without the former, the null-value branch cannot be confirmed; without the latter, the query boundary cannot be confirmed.

Still undecided: whether a conflicting explicit duration or the time points take precedence; how records missing begin or end should appear on the monthly page; and where month assignment across time zones is handled. This review did not assume any of these were resolved.

# History of null duration and monthly statistics

## 2023-05-24: A record that mixed things together

The original title was broad in scope: deriving intervals for null duration, and Inclusive Ranges for Monthly Statistics. Both issues had been observed around time-related pages, so they were initially placed in the same record. The thinking at the time was that, since begin, end, interval had all appeared, a single line of investigation should be enough to wrap things up.

Of the options listed at the time, the first was to continue requiring callers to write duration. The advantage was that null values would not need interpretation when objects were read, and any problems could also be taken back to the submitter to have the field filled in. The downside was just as direct: if the same time entry was created through different entry points, one might save duration, while another might save only the start and end times. The data shape received by pages or reports would no longer be consistent.

The second option was to treat a time entry whose explicit value was null as an interval to be derived: if begin and end were already present, the elapsed time would be obtained from those two timestamps. The initial draft described this only as a working hypothesis, because it had not yet distinguished between "the field is null" and "insufficient time information". The endpoints for monthly statistics were not settled at that point either.

In this early write-up, the mistake was to treat "being able to calculate a duration" and "which month it should belong to" as a single follow-up step. Traces of this wording are retained now, not to perpetuate it, but to explain why the two had to be separated later.

The earlier investigation started with `public/build/calendar.52d75f80.js`. The record located this build artifact by following terms such as duration, null, begin, end, interval and seconds. It was useful for looking back at snippets the pages had once used, but it left no reference chain from each caller back to the domain object. Nor was it established where monthly statistics should be implemented, just because they were on the same page of the record.

## Gaps in the initial definitions

The first version did not define "missing endpoints". It only said that a null duration could be handled by looking at the time interval, which could easily be read as meaning that having begin was enough to proceed. In fact, when begin is present but end is missing, the input is not the same as one with both endpoints present.

The first version also did not explain what a zero value meant. If an input that could not form an interval was converted to zero seconds, later readers would see a number, but would not know whether it represented an actual zero duration, or indicated that the object was missing time information. This issue was not addressed at the time, and only a note was left in the margin saying "a record with an input and a return value is needed".

For monthly statistics, only two approaches were initially noted: one used the start of the next month as the endpoint, while the other used the last point in time that could be included in the current month. Without examples spanning month boundaries, both looked like reasonable "closed intervals". The early record contained no evidence that either one applied to all reports.

## Summer of 2023: Split by input rather than by page

The first review did not begin by investigating page totals, but instead divided time-entry inputs into three groups. The first group already had an explicit duration. The second group had a null duration, but both begin and end were present. The third group had only one timestamp, or lacked the time objects needed to form an interval.

This classification yields a judgment that still holds: an empty duration does not equal no duration. The second group is missing a saved explicit value, not time information; only the third group is the case where elapsed seconds cannot be derived from the existing inputs. The first group should not be recalculated by the empty-value branch.

During the review, the third group was also deliberately not converted to zero. This does not make the page easier to explain; instead, it erases the incompleteness of the record. An input missing end cannot be disguised as an interval from begin to begin simply because the system wants to keep displaying a number.

This layer only handles input shape. It does not specify whether a missing endpoint should display as blank, an error, or some other status; the material contains no corresponding result. It also does not include cases where the explicit duration is inconsistent with begin/end. A conflicting value is not an empty value, so the empty-value branch cannot be used as a shortcut to decide which one overrides which.

The monthly question was split out as a separate concern in this review. Interval calculation answers "How long did this record run?"; month filtering answers "Which month's content does the query treat this record as?" The same cross-month record may trigger both, but the former answer does not automatically produce the latter answer.

## The trial calculation recorded was not the complete rule set

A subsequent trial calculation retained begin and end while not providing an explicit duration. The record did not preserve the complete execution command or test output; it only left a search trace for `getDuration()`, along with a manual-calculation prompt covering 10:00 to 11:30.

The value of this trial was limited but clear: it moved the inspection point from monthly totals back to reading the duration of an individual work entry. If the duration access point has not correctly interpreted the two time points, the number seen on the reporting side is not sufficient to infer whether there is a problem with the boundaries.

The trial did not cover records with only begin, nor records where the explicit duration conflicts with the interval length. It cannot support the expanded claim that "all empty values are derived." Even less can it support the claim that "deriving empty values has resolved monthly statistics."

An old note wrote the manual example as "90 minutes, which can serve as a seconds check." At the time, this was merely a manual conversion hint, not a saved interface result. Someone later read this sentence as meaning that month attribution had already been verified, causing the discussion to return to the page total. This extrapolation had no basis and is no longer used.

## The old operation left in place

The following was the troubleshooting sequence at the time; it was later explicitly deprecated, but the original text is retained:

> Read duration first; when it is empty, read begin; then fill in end from the calendar result; finally pass the seconds to the monthly statistics. For drag-and-drop records, continue investigating along the calendar construct first.

This operation had two unverified premises. First, it assumed that the calendar result was the common source for all read entry points; second, it assumed that once the seconds were obtained, month attribution was thereby determined. The former mistakenly treated `public/build/calendar.52d75f80.js` as the sole entry point for domain behavior, while the latter mistakenly treated calculation order as a reporting rule.

This path is still useful: when revisiting the earlier investigation, you can start with the snippets related to duration, null, begin, and end to find out why the calendar data source was brought into the discussion at the time. But the path itself cannot substitute for call relationships, nor can it choose endpoints for monthly statistics.

In particular, the sentence "fill in end from the calendar results" in the old procedure no longer applies. The available material does not show that the end time can be filled in on the page side for every record that lacks end. It is retained in the historical section to prevent later readers from treating an assumption that has already been questioned as the default behavior again.

## 2024-04: The review changed the order of verification

The review compared the two locations again. If durations are filled in near the calendar data source, the drag-and-drop page may obtain complete data sooner; the trade-off is that other entry points may never pass through that data source. If derivation is placed near duration access in Timesheet, consumers do not each have to duplicate null checks; the trade-off is that the object must distinguish between cases with complete begin/end and cases with missing endpoints.

The local decision made in this review was not to remove the calendar entry point from the scope of the investigation, but to relegate it to a historical reference point. The explanation for a null duration should first be verified where the duration is accessed in Timesheet. This avoids mistakenly writing the value-filling logic of a particular page entry point as a rule for the entire object.

The review did not decide to convert all anomalous records to zero. Zero seconds should represent a duration that has already been determined; a missing end time means the input is still incomplete. If the two are conflated in monthly summaries, the page may appear stable, but anomalous data will actually be impossible to identify.

The brief sequence recorded in the meeting notes was: first look at the input, interval result, and reporting month of a single record side by side, then discuss closed intervals. It is not an operations manual, much less a promise about how the query will be implemented. It only requires that a single monthly total not be used in discussions to stand in for all three types of information at once.

The same round also retained a counterexample: a record has begin, no end, and no explicit duration. It cannot yield a reliable elapsed time. If the two time points are treated as identical to keep the monthly chart producing numbers, a zero duration will mask the gap in the input; if an end point is filled in arbitrarily, external guesswork is instead written into the model. No decision is made here to fill in missing values by default.

## Why the monthly boundaries are still undecided

"Closed interval" has consistently referred to monthly query endpoints in this record, not to the subtraction used to calculate duration. Monthly examples should at least distinguish the last includable instant of the current month, the first instant of the next month, and the month to which a record spanning months belongs; using only records entirely within a month cannot reveal the differences.

Using the start of the next month as the end point for the current month was considered. It sounds simple, but records exactly at the first instant of the next month may overlap with the query for the next month. Another candidate is to cut off at the last includable point in time of the current month. This avoids the obvious overlap, but the actual query precision and time zone handling still need to be confirmed.

Therefore, neither candidate has been written as a global rule at this point. Monthly statistics cannot recalculate a null duration, nor can they assume that the month assignment is known just because the duration has already been determined. The interval branches and month filtering each need their own examples.

This is not avoidance of a decision. The decision concerns ordering and boundaries of responsibility: the Timesheet duration accessor is responsible for interpreting the available begin/end; monthly statistics is responsible for validating its own filtering endpoint. Without new cross-month records and returned results, do not promote historical candidates to implementation requirements.

## 2025 year field feedback: revising the old conclusion

The latest field feedback rechecked the manual examples from 10:00 through 11:30. The old record only described it as a "90 minutes" hint. Later, some people in the discussion treated this hint as meaning that the seconds calculation had been finalized, while others extrapolated it to monthly boundaries. Both readings went beyond the old material.

After revision, the example is used only to check interval calculations for a null explicit value; it no longer serves as evidence for monthly statistics. During calculation, begin and end should not be modified in order to obtain elapsed seconds. Time points are inputs, elapsed time is a read result, and the derivation must not be written as a patch to the original time objects.

This feedback also invalidated an old claim: early records said, "filling in values around the calendar is enough to avoid differences among different entry points." It overlooked that other read entry points might bypass page artifacts. This sentence is now retained as a disproven working hypothesis and is no longer used to determine object behavior.

From this point on, searches for `getDuration()` no longer center on calendar artifacts, but on the Timesheet duration accessor. The artifact path can still help locate the old notes; it is not proof of the current decision's ownership.

## Current decision

After the earlier starting-point record, input classification, trial calculations, old operations, review addendum, and field correction, the current position is as follows:

> When a Timesheet has a null explicit duration, getDuration() derives elapsed seconds from begin and end; a 10:00 to 11:30 interval returns 5400 without changing either timestamp.

This decision covers only Timesheets with a null explicit duration and both begin and end available. It specifies the source of the elapsed seconds; it does not create default values for any missing fields. When begin or end is missing, the record remains unprocessed input; when explicit duration already exists, it also does not enter this branch.

"without changing either timestamp" is also part of the decision. The calculation reads begin and end without changing them to interval boundaries, the current time, or computed replacement values. If a caller needs to repair incomplete records, that must be handled by separately defined write rules, not as part of reading the duration.

This decision does not specify precedence in a conflict. If an explicit duration exists but differs from the difference calculated from begin/end, this page provides no basis for saying which overrides which. Conflicting values must not be assigned to the null explicit duration branch just to make the boundary cases look complete.

The interval branches can be reviewed in the following state diagram:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ExplicitDuration
    [*] --> EmptyDuration
    ExplicitDuration --> ReturnedDuration
    EmptyDuration --> BeginAndEndAvailable
    BeginAndEndAvailable --> ReturnedDuration
    EmptyDuration --> MissingEndpoint
    MissingEndpoint --> Unresolved
```

In the diagram, `ExplicitDuration` marks the entry points that this decision does not address. `EmptyDuration` reaches `ReturnedDuration` only when both endpoints are present. `MissingEndpoint` remains `Unresolved`, and is neither an alias for zero seconds nor a signal that the calendar data source should automatically repair it.

## Scope of the Decision on Monthly Statistics

Inclusive Ranges for Monthly Statistics is still not defined as a final implementation rule in this record. The current decision only requires monthly checks not to duplicate their own derivation logic for null duration. If pages, reports, and other callers each interpret null values independently, the same time entry may yield different durations depending on the entry point.

Monthly checks need inputs that span months, especially records whose end point falls exactly at the first instant of the next month. Only examples like these can distinguish between the two candidates of "using the start of the next month as the end point" and "using the last countable instant of the current month as the end point". Using only 10:00 to 11:30 within the same month as a monthly boundary example is meaningless; it can only test the duration branch.

Until the monthly materials are complete, two restrictions remain here. First, do not substitute the interval length in seconds for validation of month attribution. Second, do not use examples entirely within a month to prove that an interval is closed. These would miss cross-month endpoints and query overlap issues, respectively.

## Related Issues Not Yet Split Out

- When an explicit duration conflicts with begin/end, which value governs subsequent reports.
- How the monthly page should represent time entries missing begin or end.
- For month attribution of records spanning time zones, whether to convert before aggregation or handle it on the query side.
- Whether the calendar data source in `public/build/calendar.52d75f80.js` still corresponds to an actual call entry point.

The last item cannot be answered from the path name. The old record can show that the search started here at the time, but it cannot show that all reads pass through here. The first three items also cannot be assumed to be resolved merely because the current interval branch already has well-defined behavior.

## Retained Review Excerpts

> Don't turn "closed intervals" into a complete set of reporting rules just yet. Get the examples with an empty duration right first, then use cross-month data to examine the endpoints.

This excerpt preserves the sequence in which the discussion converged at the time. It explains why this page first establishes clear boundaries for reading durations, while keeping the month-related issue as a separate candidate. It provides no additional answers on missing end values, conflicting duration values, or time zone assignment.

Another review margin note reads: "Do not just paste the page total." The reason is that totals cannot show whether a record has an explicit duration, whether both endpoints are present, and which month's query actually included the record. This requirement still applies to subsequent monthly reviews.

## Appendix of Old Examples

### Example One: The Same Hour

The old note uses 09:00 to 10:00 to illustrate that "having begin and end gives you one hour". This example can help distinguish an empty explicit value from a complete interval, but it is too simple to establish whether monthly queries use closed intervals. It is no longer used as a basis for monthly boundaries.

### Example Two: The Last Minute Across Months

The old proposal passed the interval from 23:59 at month-end to 00:01 in the following month directly into the monthly statistics, with "archive by end time" written alongside it. That statement was later marked as no longer applicable: it did not specify the query range, nor did it handle records exactly at the first instant of the following month. The example is retained as a reminder that subsequent reviews must not rely solely on an archiving description.

### Example Three: Only a Start Time

This is an old example that has never been fully addressed: it has begin, but no end and no explicit duration. It is still treated as `Unresolved`. A seemingly reasonable end time must not be filled in, nor should the issue be concealed with zero seconds. If records of this type are included in monthly statistics in the future, both calculation and presentation must be specified, rather than merely adding a default value.

### Example Four: Mismatch Between the Explicit Value and the Interval

An earlier discussion tried to treat this kind of record as "a special case of derivation from null values". That classification has been abandoned. It has an explicit duration, so it does not meet the precondition of the current decision; which value should account for the discrepancy still needs separate confirmation. This example is retained to prevent callers from pushing conflicting values back into the null-value branch.

## Where to Look

To revisit the historical investigation, start with the snippets related to duration, null, begin, and end in `public/build/calendar.52d75f80.js`. It preserves the search entry points around the old page. The current decision concerns Timesheet's duration access behavior; Inclusive Ranges for Monthly Statistics is still awaiting cross-month inputs and actual returned results. The old examples in the appendix are intended to identify past judgments, not to replace new month-related validation.

# Proposal for work-hour thresholds and language changes

This interface review brings together two seemingly unrelated issues: where to enforce limits on long time entries, and who should handle duplicates and an empty default in the language list. The former affects time entry and existing validation; the latter can lead to mistaking configuration order for business semantics.

Start by considering smaller changes. The threshold should not be hard-coded in callers; one option is to read it from the time-tracking configuration and have the validation object handle it. This would let administrators adjust the limit without changing call sites, but we first need to confirm the threshold's unit and whether records with no end time should be rejected by the same rule. The old draft provisionally treated "validate whenever duration is large enough" as a working assumption; there were no counterexamples to that assumption yet.

For the language list, per-caller deduplication is not recommended. One option is to deduplicate in the language service before returning the list, and decide what to return if the default language is not in the available set. It hasn't been decided whether to keep the first or last occurrence of a duplicate, and there isn't enough information to say which language to fall back to when the default is empty.

At the time, public/build/app.1cecb23c.js could be used to look back at nearby names. Here, treat it as a lookup starting point, not as a basis for determining implementation ownership.

Withdrawal conditions: If the threshold configuration cannot express the existing business limits, or deduplication changes the existing default-language selection, limit the work to caller samples and hold off on merging these two changes.

# Duration Threshold and Language Changes Proposal

Long-duration time entries and the language service were initially discussed together because both raised the question of "who decides the default behavior." On review, that framing was too broad: the duration limit concerns the validation boundary for a completed time entry; the language list concerns cleaning up a collection of configuration values. They remain on the same page to record why we considered changing them together at the time, not to present them as a single mechanism.

## Revising the threshold approach

The first draft's working assumption was that any record with a duration should be subject to the limit. That would pull records still being timed, without a complete duration yet, into the same check. The review to date does not support expanding the scope this way, so that statement in the draft is no longer a premise of the proposal.

A narrower option is to put the threshold in the time-entry configuration and have the constraint and its corresponding validator read it; callers provide only the time-entry object and do not convert the limit themselves. This would avoid separate upper limits for the web UI, API, and import paths. The trade-off is that the interpretation of configuration values must be fixed. In particular, callers must not have to guess what zero, negative, and unset values mean.

Three places for the check were listed at the time:

- Compare directly before form submission; the change is straightforward, but misses non-form entry points.
- Compare during the save operation; broader coverage, but ties the timing of feedback to persistence.
- Compare during constraint validation; requires a clear definition of what counts as "completed," but lets different entry points share the same semantics.

The preference is for the third option. This is not a commitment to refactor all duration rules; it applies only to the long-duration limit. If reading the configuration fails, the threshold units differ across callers, or multiple identical limit errors are reported for one record, the approach should revert to the original entry points; more examples should be collected before deciding.

public/build/app.1cecb23c.js can still be used to look up which names appeared next to each other at the time. It is an entry point into an old revision and cannot be used as proof that callers subsequently migrated. The earlier interpretation that the names seen there directly represented the final relationships was an overreach and has been removed from this version.

## Language changes remain undecided

The goal of the language service is not to normalize all regional preferences into a single value. Only two questions are under discussion: whether duplicate entries in the available-language list should be reduced to one, and how to expose the state when the default language is not in that list. The former is better suited to handling within the service; the latter affects the default value callers see and cannot be decided merely as a side effect of deduplicating the list.

Two ordering rules were left open in the review: keep the first occurrence, or let later configuration override earlier entries. Keeping the first occurrence is closer to the intuition of "configuration declaration order"; the latter makes local overrides easier. Without results from callers, neither rule will be specified as settled interface behavior. An empty default value also remains an empty entry; the first language must not be picked arbitrarily just to populate the UI.

The tentative trial is limited to the collection returned by the language service. Withdraw it if any of the following occurs: the default value changes after deduplication, the duplicate entries themselves carry different regional meanings, or callers depend on the ordering of duplicate entries. Evidence from real calls and user-visible behavior needs to be added before deciding whether the default value should be part of the same change.

## Open questions

- If the threshold configuration is missing, should the constraint skip the check or report a configuration issue?
- Does determining whether a record is complete depend only on duration, or also on its end status?
- When the default language is invalid, do callers need an empty value, the original value, or some other explicit state?

This proposal preserves the record of the first draft's combined discussion, but no longer argues that the two tracks must ship together.
versions.change_summary: Narrowed the threshold scope; kept the language questions open

# Work-Hours Threshold and Language Adjustment Proposal

The original goal of this page was to leave a proposal that could be withdrawn for a round of interface review, not to provide a general overview of work-hours rules or localization configuration. Two workstreams were placed side by side at the time: one concerned where long-duration time entries should actually be evaluated, and the other concerned where the default should be determined when supported languages contain duplicates. In retrospect, the two shared only the timing of the review, not an implementation boundary.

The older version is still mentioned in some troubleshooting records because it preserves the original disagreements about configuration placement and caller-side risks. Not all of its conclusions remain suitable to carry forward unchanged: in particular, the first draft started from "all entries with duration undergo long-duration validation," which mixes incomplete entries with entries whose full duration has already been established. The reasoning behind that judgment is retained below, with the parts that have since been revised kept near their original locations.

## What We Initially Wanted to Address

The first version proposed removing the upper limit from web pages and interface call sites and placing it in the work-hours rule configuration. The motivation was straightforward: if the same upper limit is scattered across multiple entry points, each entry point may retain its old value after the limit is changed in the admin interface. The draft therefore listed three candidate locations: a pre-form comparison, a save-time comparison, and constraint validation.

At the time, there were not enough records to distinguish "in-progress time entries" from "completed time entries." The draft used the presence or absence of duration as a substitute for that distinction and assumed that all entry points should provide the same message when they detected that the limit had been exceeded. This passage is retained below to make the later correction easier to understand:

> Old assumption: whenever an entry has duration, it is handled by the limit check; callers do not need to distinguish entry states.

That assumption was not retained. duration is only a numeric value and cannot stand in for completion status; using it as the sole gate would cause the rule to intervene too early during entry. The original text was not removed because it explains why the early proposal emphasized "the validator covers all entry points," and also why the object's state later needed to be stated explicitly.

## Trade-offs Retained During the Review

The review did not expand the threshold into a general work-hours policy. The discussion remained focused on the long-duration limit, and there were still three candidate locations, but the trade-offs became somewhat more specific.

A pre-form comparison lets users see a message earlier, but does not naturally cover non-form calls. Placing the check in the save action covers a broader range of entry points, but entangles the meaning of errors with persistence outcomes: callers have difficulty distinguishing whether the entry itself is invalid or the save process failed. Placing it in the constraint object lets different entry points evaluate the same object; the cost is that the constraint must explicitly state which configuration layer to read, which units to use, and when not to produce an error.

This page therefore favored the constraint side at the time. Here, "favored" does not mean that all old checks must be migrated there, nor does it claim that every caller has already been updated. It simply rejects having each caller interpret the upper limit independently. If the configuration hierarchy cannot express the limit consistently, or the same entry receives duplicate messages in a single validation run, this consolidation should be rolled back, first reverting to the existing entry points and collecting enough samples.

Someone once suggested treating zero, negative numbers, and missing values as unlimited, on the grounds that this would be the easiest way to stay compatible with old configurations. This suggestion was not recorded as a formal decision. It collapses three different cases into the same meaning: a missing configuration may be a deployment omission, zero may mean an explicit disablement, and a negative number may simply be invalid input. Without actual configuration samples, a single permissive rule cannot be used to classify them.

## The Lookup Starting Point at the Time

public/build/app.1cecb23c.js is an old starting point retained in this set of records. It is useful for finding declarations that were adjacent at the time using issue names and call names, but not for determining from path location who owns the rule, who has integrated it, or whether later versions still follow the same code path. An early review misread name adjacency as a call relationship; this page later revised that assessment to "available for reference" and no longer treated it as evidence of ownership.

This also affected how the proposal was presented. The work-hours section only identifies a candidate boundary on the constraint side; it does not connect symbols found in build artifacts into a complete call graph. Likewise, the language section does not infer all clients' default-language policies from a single service name. Both subjects need actual call results, but the results that still need to be supplied differ.

## The Language Workstream Remains an Unfinished Proposal

The discussion of supported languages arose because the list might contain duplicate items, and the default language might not be in the cleaned-up set. Initially, someone advocated handling both together: the service would first deduplicate the list, then fill in the default using the first item after deduplication. This proposal seemed convenient, but it would tie "cleaning up the display list" to "the user or system default."

The narrower idea retained after the review was: duplicate items can be consolidated when the language service returns the collection, but whether a default exists, is empty, or needs to be preserved as its original value is a separate interface choice. Without results from callers, the list becoming shorter is not a reason to choose a fallback language unilaterally.

Two ordering rules remain undecided here. Keeping the first occurrence more closely follows the configuration's declaration order; keeping the last occurrence allows later configuration to override earlier values. Either can be reasonable, depending on whether the duplicates are merely the same language code or carry different local intent. The old proposal did not make this distinction, so it cannot be used to directly determine current behavior.

Further investigation can start with App\Utils\LanguageService, focusing on how callers use getDefaultLanguage, and what role isKnownLanguage plays before and after the default is determined. This record lists them only as areas to inspect; until the calling patterns are documented in full, the language section remains a trial proposal.

The conditions for withdrawing the language workstream should also be handled independently: if deduplication changes the default, duplicate items carry different regional meanings, or callers depend on the original ordering of duplicates, it should not be merged. It does not need to wait for joint completion with the long-duration work-hours rules, nor should it use the conclusions from work-hours validation to justify itself.

## The Contract After This Round's Narrowing

For long-duration time entries, the current contract covers only completed entries and positive thresholds; it does not also bring configuration errors, incomplete states, or other duration rules into scope. The precise interface contract is as follows: App\Validator\Constraints\TimesheetLongRunning and App\Validator\Constraints\TimesheetLongRunningValidator read timesheet.rules.long_running_duration in minutes and add exactly one violation when a completed entry exceeds a positive configured threshold.

This contract replaces the earlier ambiguous "validate whenever duration exists" with a boundary based on completed entries, and also lists duplicate messages as an unacceptable outcome. rules and long_running_duration in the configuration path are not two options for callers to interpret separately; they belong to the same read path. Continuing to copy the upper limit from other locations would return to the divergence the first version tried to avoid.

However, narrowing the scope does not settle the final handling of missing configuration, nor does it specify fallback behavior for language defaults. The former requires configuration samples to distinguish deployment omissions from explicit disablement; the latter requires actual callers to determine whether an empty value is acceptable. Leaving these gaps in the proposal is more useful than disguising them as an already settled compatibility strategy.

## Earlier Conclusions and Withdrawal Points

Only two points can still be carried forward: long-duration limits should be expressed through centralized configuration, and language deduplication should not be reimplemented separately by each caller. The parts that cannot be carried forward are "check all entries with duration" and "automatically choose the first default language after deduplication." The former has been replaced by a boundary based on completion status; the latter is not supported by evidence from callers.

If an implementation finds that the same completed entry receives more than one limit message, or that the threshold is not interpreted in minutes, this contract should no longer be used and the configuration read point should be reexamined. If language deduplication changes the default users see, the language change should also be rolled back independently, without affecting the assessment on the work-hours side.

This record still points to an old revision, so it is better suited to explaining the trade-offs and misjudgments at the time. If you need to trace language calls or introduce new configuration structures, start a separate record to capture the context rather than retroactively inserting later conclusions here.

# Calendar Limit and Start-of-Year Calculation Migration Workflow

This upgrade brought the calendar drag item count and start-of-year date handling to light at the same time because all the legacy integrations appeared in the same regression cycle. Don't treat them as one problem yet. The former is the boundary on how many candidate items drag handling can accept; the latter is whether the original date can still be used by the caller when deriving the start of the year from an existing date.

The old page behavior was to first check how many items were in the current list. When the list was short, it did not expand further; when it was long, the caller first took a subset and then passed it to the drag logic. This kept the page results stable, but it did not say whether the item limit came from configuration, the event, or the page load in question.

At the time, the legacy integrations were handled in the following order:

1. Determine whether the caller truncated the collection before creating the drag event.
2. Record the size of the slice; don't treat it directly as the event's own limit.
3. Locate the date calculation separately and confirm whether the start-of-year value is a separate calculation result or overwrites the passed-in date.
4. Make the count and date changes separately, so a page result in one area doesn't mask an issue in the other.

The old note on the date side says, "Move the date to the start of the year and pass it on." That wording isn't precise enough. If the date supplied by the caller is modified directly, later branches that read the month, date, or time no longer get the original input. Even if the year displayed on the page is correct, that doesn't show that passing the value this way is safe.

The old build entry is retained at `public/build/calendar.52d75f80.js`. You can trace the calendar integration back near `calendar`, `events`, and `count`, but the list length in the build file is only a navigation clue; it cannot replace the source of the count when the event is created.

When restoring the old page behavior, first restore the caller's own display truncation; don't write the length of the currently loaded collection back into the drag event. If range changes on the date side need to be rolled back, restore the call with the original range rather than modifying the input date again to obtain the start-of-year value.

Open item: In the old caller, were items beyond the display range not shown, processed later, or already discarded before the event was created? This distinction will affect where the page collection and count boundary should be separated during migration.
versions.change_summary: Retain the split migration order for the legacy integration

# Migrating calendar limits and start-of-year calculations

Calendar drag-and-drop items and the start-of-year timestamp were originally included in the same upgrade notes only because both were in scope for regression testing. After reviewing the legacy integrations, the two should still be kept on the same page for comparison during migration, but they must no longer be treated as the same kind of configuration issue: the item count describes the limit on downstream processing; the start-of-year calculation describes how a date value is derived and whether the date supplied by the caller is preserved.

## Early page-based assumptions

The earliest investigation in 2023 started with page behavior. Some date ranges produced shorter calendar lists, while others produced longer ones. The old notes took this to mean that the caller had already applied the count limit: first taking the collection currently visible on the page, then passing the trimmed result to the drag-and-drop logic.

The old guidance included this instruction:

> Continue processing as many items as the page can load.

This line is now retained to help identify the old branch, not as a migration rule. The length of the page's collection depends on the active range, refresh timing, and caller-side filtering; it can explain why a particular page showed only a few items, but it does not establish the maximum count allowed when creating a drag-and-drop event. The fact that the two sometimes match does not make them the same value.

Date handling used a similar simplification. The old page described "getting the start of the year" as directly adjusting the existing date and then passing that date to the subsequent range logic. With this approach, the start-of-year result looked fine, but the original month, day, and time had already been lost. If later logic still read the original input, it would get the date as modified by the earlier step.

## On-call addendum

A later addendum required each of the two lines of investigation to have its own observation points. The count check no longer just asks how many items the page displays. It first asks whether the caller trims the collection itself, then where the count passed in at event creation is retained, and only then what value subscribers use to determine their processing range.

For the date check, inspect the state of the same input before and after the calculation. The focus is not whether the start-of-year result falls in January, but whether the date originally supplied by the caller still retains its original year, month, day, and time after the calculation. The return value can be used in the annual range calculation; this step should not change what the input represents.

These two checks cannot be combined into a single UI acceptance check. An incorrect count limit commonly shows up as too many or too few items being processed; a modified input date may not cause a problem until later range checks, page repopulation, or comparison logic. Checking only whether the calendar can render makes it easy to miss the latter.

## Discarded transitional changes

One attempted change wrote the number of items already loaded on the page back into the drag-and-drop event. The rationale was to have the page and subscribers see the same number, seemingly removing one variable from the investigation. This change was not kept. The page's loaded item count is runtime state that can change with the date range or caller-side filtering; the event needs to carry the limit agreed on at creation. Writing the former into the latter gives downstream code only the number the page happened to have loaded at that point.

For dates, another attempt adjusted the input object directly to the start of the year. It removed one local variable, but merged the derived result and the caller's input into a single mutable object. The start-of-year value itself might be correct, but the ability to read the original date later was already lost.

The shared problem with these two attempts was not page behavior, but treating an easily available local value as a long-lived boundary: the page's collection cannot stand in for event parameters, and an adjusted date cannot stand in for the original input.

## Migrating away from the legacy integration

Start the migration by checking `public/build/calendar.52d75f80.js` for the legacy calendar entry points. In that file, `calendar`, `events`, and `count` can be used to find the areas around historical calls; the actual event creation and subscription points, and whether caller-side trimming happens before or after them, still need to be confirmed.

Recommended migration order:

- Keep a record of the caller's existing display trimming, including where it happens; do not use the length of the trimmed collection to define the event's limit.
- Keep a separate maximum-count value on the path that creates drag-and-drop events.
- Have subscribers read this count from the event, then determine their own processing range.
- Use a separate date result for the start-of-year calculation; keep the original date for subsequent branches that need the month, day, or time.
- Commit the count and date changes separately. Either change can then be reverted independently during regression testing while retaining the observations from the other.

If legacy callers cannot migrate immediately, they can temporarily continue trimming the collection in the display layer. This transition affects only the page display and should not overwrite the count carried by the drag-and-drop event. Otherwise, page state will once again become an implicit limit for downstream code.

## Rollback paths

If the only difference after the upgrade is the number of items displayed on the page, first check whether caller-side display trimming was removed or moved. The display branch can be restored while keeping the independent count in the event. Do not write the current collection length into the event just to restore the old page appearance.

If downstream code processes an unexpected number of items, go back to the event creation code and confirm the source of the count, then check whether subscribers read the same value. Expanding the page's load range cannot fix an incorrect source for the limit, because the load range only changes the collection; it does not define the maximum number of items allowed to be processed.

If the annual range shifts, first confirm whether the start-of-year calculation has modified the original input date. Being able to get January 1 again does not mean the processing is correct; also confirm that subsequent logic depending on the original month, day, or time has not received the derived object. A rollback should restore the range call rather than rely on modifying the input date as a workaround.

## Open questions from review

The review confirmed that the "configured count" and the "currently loaded count" must be distinguished, but did not confirm whether every legacy subscriber reads directly from the event object. Some legacy integrations may still infer their processing range from the page's collection and need to be identified one by one during migration.

When time zones are involved in the annual range, this page also leaves open which layer should decide which year a date belongs to. This page records only that deriving the start of the year should not modify the input object; the time zone used for range transitions still needs to be checked at the date call site.

## Retained legacy notes

An old note said there was no need to investigate count limits further if the calendar displayed correctly. That statement no longer applies. A normal display only shows that the current collection can be rendered; it does not show that the limit established at event creation still exists.

Another old note assumed that callers only cared about the year, so the date could be overwritten directly. That assumption is no longer used either. This migration record does not support assuming that callers care only about the year, much less using that assumption to ignore later branches that read the original date.
versions.change_summary: Added back the earlier approach, rollback branches, and open review questions.
